food.text: In the Old Russian period, the main foods were bread, grains, and other starchy foods. At gatherings, a loaf of bread and salt was always present on the table.

Shchi, a cabbage soup, was the predominant first course in Russian cuisine for over a thousand years. It knew no class boundaries. The rich used richer ingredients, while the poor made it solely of cabbage and onions.

Russian peasant food grew out of a harsh climate and combined plentiful fish, pork, poultry, caviar, mushrooms, berries, and honey. Crops of rye, wheat, barley and millet supplied breads, pancakes, pies, cereals, beer and vodka.

Under Polish-Lithuanian rule in the late medieval period, Ukrainian cooking developed as part of the wider food culture of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Historian Oleksii Sokyrko notes that cereals and bread stayed the base of most people's diet. Peas and beans were also widely eaten, especially in Galicia.
The distinctive taste of shchi came from letting it draw, or stew, in a Russian stove after cooking. The "spirit of shchi" was seen as inseparable from the Russian izba, the log hut.
Kasha made from grains such as buckwheat and oats was seen as a sign of wellbeing for the household. It was a lasting staple of the Russian table.
Many Russians combined honey and berries to make gingerbread. It is still a popular Russian dessert today.
Many Russian proverbs are connected to shchi. One says Shchi da kasha, pishcha nasha, meaning "Shchi and porridge are our staples". The soup could be eaten regularly and at any time of the year.

art.text: The Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos in Suzdal is a World Heritage Site and one of the eight White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal. It is described as one of the most complex monuments of Russian medieval architecture.
art.source_title: Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos, Suzdal
tags: White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal

art.text: Russian vernacular architecture stems from wooden construction traditions, and monumental masonry construction began to appear during the Kievan period. After the Mongol invasions, Russian architecture continued in successor states including Novgorod, Vladimir-Suzdal, Pskov and Moscow.

Built between 1045 and 1050 under the patronage of Vladimir Yaroslavich, the Saint Sophia Cathedral in Novgorod is the oldest structure still in use in Russia. Its austere stone walls and five helmet-shaped domes were the first to display features that came to define Russian architecture.

The Yuriev Monastery near Novgorod, one of Russia's oldest monasteries, gained a tall three-domed cathedral in 1119. It was built by Vsevolod, son of Mstislav the Great, together with Kyurik, the monastery's head.

The Suzdal cathedral was first built during the reign of Vladimir II Monomakh in 1102. In 1222, Yuri II of Vladimir ordered the dilapidated building demolished and replaced with a new one of white tufa stone decorated with limestone.
art.source_title: Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos, Suzdal

art.text: Very little secular architecture of Kievan Rus' has survived. Until the 20th century only the Golden Gates of Vladimir could be regarded as an authentic pre-Mongol monument, despite much 18th-century restoration.

In 1474, Ivan III imported builders from Pskov to Moscow. Pskov had been saved from ruin by the Mongol horde and so had more advanced construction knowledge, and its builders adapted the stone-slab method to the brick masonry of Moscow's churches.

The bronze gates of Saint Sophia Cathedral were long believed to have been cast in Magdeburg in 1156, with some accounts instead tracing them to Płock in Poland. More recent scholarship holds that Archbishop Euthymius II, who led the Novgorod church from 1429 to 1458, likely purchased them in the mid-15th century.

A similar three-domed cathedral was completed in 1117 at the Antoniev Monastery, on the orders of its founder Antony. It was probably designed by the same masters who built the Yuriev Monastery's cathedral two years later.

The Cathedral of the Nativity in Suzdal is notable for being the first city cathedral not built for the exclusive use of the knyaz or his relatives. It contains the remains of a son of Yuri Dolgoruki and of knyazes of the Shuisky family.
art.source_title: Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos, Suzdal

art.text: When the Mongols sacked Suzdal in 1238, the interior of the Cathedral of the Nativity was destroyed. The building survived centuries of the Tatar-Mongol yoke, but finally burned down and collapsed in 1445.
art.source_title: Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos, Suzdal

art.text: In the early 12th century, several princely churches were built in a more simplistic form of the Cathedral of St Sophia. Examples include the Cathedral of St. Nicholas in Yaroslav's Court (1113) and the Church of the Nativity of the Virgin at Antoniev Monastery (1117 to 1119).

The Church of the Holy Spirit (1476) shows a bold Muscovite tendency toward ornament, with a frieze made of glazed ceramic tiles. The frieze derives from the ornamental stripes of Novgorod, Pskov and Suzdalia.

Outside the Novgorod Kremlin, at Yaroslav's Court, St. Nicholas Cathedral was built between 1113 and 1123 during the reign of Mstislav the Great. Its walls still preserve frescoes portraying members of Mstislav's own family.
During the 1940s, archaeologist Nikolai Voronin discovered the well-preserved remains of Andrey Bogolyubsky's palace in Bogolyubovo. The palace dates from 1158 to 1165.

Pskov builders also worked on the Church of the Deposition of the Robe (1484 to 1485), which shows ornamental brickwork in its façade. Ivan III's reign also produced fortifications, the Ivan the Great Bell Tower, and the Palace of Facets.
tags: Church of the Deposition of the Robe

war.text: On 8 September 1380, Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow defeated the Mongol commander Mamai of the Golden Horde at Kulikovo Field, near the Don River, after a cruel, long melee in which an "innumerable multitude of people" perished on both sides. A third of the commanders of the 23 "banners" were killed. Dmitry survived, wounded and fainting from exhaustion, but his entire escort had died or scattered, and he was hardly found among the corpses. The victorious army stood "on the bones" for six days, and Dmitry became known as Donskoy, meaning "of the Don".

On 31 May 1223, a Mongol army led by Jebe and Subutai crushed a coalition of Rus' principalities and Cumans on the banks of the Kalka River. The Rus' were commanded jointly by Mstislav the Bold and Mstislav III of Kiev. The defeat was ruinous: the Novgorodian First Chronicle says only 1 in 10 soldiers made it back home, while the Primary Chronicle gives 10,000 killed and the much later, less reliable Nikonian Chronicle 60,000.
Led by Prince Alexander Nevsky, the Novgorodians repelled invading Swedes in the Battle of the Neva in 1240. In 1242 they defeated Germanic crusaders in the Battle on the Ice.

Kievan Rus' fell to the Mongol invasions of 1237 to 1238, which overran much of the region. They sacked Kiev in 1240 and other cities, and killed a significant portion of the population. The invaders, later known as Tatars, formed the Golden Horde, which ruled over Russia for the next two centuries. Only the Novgorod Republic escaped foreign occupation, by agreeing to pay tribute to the Mongols.

The victory at Kulikovo did not end Mongol domination over Russia. It is traditionally seen as the turning point when Mongol influence began to wane and Moscow's power began to rise. The Great Stand on the Ugra River in 1480 marked another important turning point.

At Kalka, the Rus' pursued the Mongols for several days as they feigned a retreat, which spread out the Rus' armies. The Mongols then stopped and formed up on the banks of the Kalka River. Mstislav the Bold and his Cuman allies attacked without waiting for the rest of the army and were defeated. The Cumans broke and ran through the Rus' ranks, causing mass confusion and being slaughtered by the Mongols. The Mongol wings then closed around the shattered Rus' army, cutting off its retreat, and hit the surrounded men with volley after volley of arrows and cavalry charges at any weakness.

In 1371, Mamai gave Prince Mikhail of Tver a jarliq to the Grand Duchy of Vladimir. Moscow's troops simply did not let the new "Grand Prince" enter Vladimir, despite the presence of a Tatar ambassador. The jarliq later returned to Dmitry.

When Mamai again gave Tver a jarliq for the Grand Duchy in 1375, Dmitry moved quickly on Tver with a strong army, larger than the one at Kulikovo. Tver capitulated, and Mikhail recognized himself as the "little brother" of the prince of Moscow.

After the defeat at Kalka, Mstislav of Kiev retreated to a fortified camp and held out for three days under Mongol siege. He then surrendered in return for a promise of safe conduct for himself and his men. Once they surrendered, the Mongols slaughtered them. Mstislav and the Kievan nobles were executed in the traditional Mongol way for royalty, without shedding blood: they were buried and suffocated under the Mongol general's victory platform while the Mongols held their victory feast.

In 1377, "Mamai's tatars" defeated the army of Nizhny Novgorod at the Battle on Pyana River, despite an auxiliary detachment left by Dmitry. The Tatars then began to raid Nizhny Novgorod and Ryazan. That same year, Moscow's troops had seized the city of Bolghar.

In 1441, the Genghisid prince Haci I Giray founded the Crimean Khanate on the Crimean Peninsula and the surrounding steppes. The Khanate orchestrated Tatar slave raids. Over the next three centuries, the Crimean slave trade would enslave an estimated two million people in the region.

literature.text: The main type of Old Russian historical literature was the chronicle, and most chronicles were anonymous. The oldest is the Primary Chronicle, also called the Tale of Nestor the Chronicler, dated to around 1115.
Medieval Russian literature had an overwhelmingly religious character. It was written in an adapted form of the Church Slavonic language that contained many South Slavic elements.

Bylina are Russian oral epic poems whose stories are loosely based on historical fact but greatly embellished with fantasy or hyperbole. They originate from the times of Kievan Rus', yet by the time they were collected they had survived only in northern Russia.

The oldest dated book of Kievan Rus, the Ostromir Gospels, was completed in 1056 or 1057. It was written by a deacon named Gregory for his patron Ostromir, the posadnik of Novgorod, probably to be given as a gift to a monastery.

In 2000, archaeologists in Novgorod uncovered a palimpsest of wax-covered wooden tablets known as the Novgorod Codex. Dating evidence places its writing in the first quarter of the 11th century, making it the oldest known book of the Kievan Rus', older than the Ostromir Gospels.

In the mid-11th century, Metropolitan Hilarion of Kiev wrote his Sermon on Law and Grace, confirming the basics of Kievan Rus' new Christian world outlook. Yet he used the Turkic title khagan five times, applying it to both Vladimir the Great and Yaroslav the Wise.
The monk Nestor entered the Kyivan Cave Monastery at age 17. In the 1080's he became known for writing the Account about the Life and Martyrdom of the Blessed Passion Bearers Boris and Gleb.

Hagiographies, or lives of the saints, were a popular genre in Old Russian literature. The first notable hagiographer was Nestor the Chronicler, who wrote about Boris and Gleb, the first saints of Kievan Rus', and about the abbot Theodosius.

The Tale of Igor's Campaign is an anonymous prose poem from the 12th century, regarded as a masterpiece of Old Russian literature. It sits alongside other anonymous works such as Praying of Daniel the Immured.

The Ostromir Gospels of 1056 to 1057 are the earliest dated manuscript to contain Russian elements. They mark the beginning of Russianized Church Slavonic, which would gradually spread to liturgical, ecclesiastical and chancery texts.

Because its wax-covered pages could be smoothed clean, the Novgorod Codex was reused over and over. Its owner wrote down dozens, probably hundreds, of different texts on the same tablets across two or three decades, wiping out each one before writing the next.

The Life of Alexander Nevsky is a well-known example of Old Russian hagiography. It combines political realism with hagiographical ideals and concentrates on the key events of Alexander Nevsky's political career.
The earliest account of a pilgrimage in Old Russian literature is The Pilgrimage of the Abbot Daniel. It records the journey of Daniel the Traveller to the Holy Land.
Complex epic works such as The Tale of the Destruction of Ryazan recall the havoc caused by the Mongol invasions. It shows how Old Russian literature responded to the catastrophe.
tags: Tale of the Destruction of Ryazan

literature.text: Scholar Charles J. Halperin argued that Hilarion's use of a 'steppe title' in Kiev may be the only case of the title's use by a non-nomadic people. He found it 'highly anomalous' that a Christian prelate would laud his ruler with a shamanist title. Halperin and Peter B. Golden saw it as a sign of Khazar influence on Kievan Rus'.

The birch bark manuscripts of the 11th to 15th centuries come closest to the vernacular Old Russian language. They show more evidence of a native Russian idiom than the Church Slavonic of formal texts.

Russell Zguta argues that after Christianization, puritan clerics pushed the court poets called gusliari and the flamboyant minstrels called skomorokhi out of Kiev. The two traditions merged and fled north to places such as Novgorod and Vladimir, where their byliny survived.

politics.text: Kievan Rus' became the largest and most powerful state in Europe in the 10th and 11th centuries, a period known as its Golden Age. Under Yaroslav the Wise, who ruled from 1019 to 1054, it reached the peak of its cultural development and military power. The state soon fragmented as regional powers rose again.

The Mongols swept through the Rus' lands in 1237 to 1238, burning the city of Vladimir on 4 February 1238 and routing the Russians at the Sit' River. By then they had conquered most of the Russian principalities. Only the Novgorod Republic escaped occupation and continued to flourish in the orbit of the Hanseatic League.

Ivan III, who ruled from 1462 to 1505, laid the groundwork of the Russian state. He expanded his domain, established a centralized national state, and secured independence from the Great Horde. His grandson Ivan IV was later the first Russian monarch crowned as tsar, in 1547.

The Novgorod Republic formally won its independence in 1136 and was an exception to the tradition of strong princely rule. From the mid-13th century the grand princes of Vladimir held its throne, but the prince's authority gradually faded. Political power increasingly passed to the veche, a popular assembly, and to elected officials.

After the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054, the Rurikid house underwent a major schism. It divided into three branches descended from three successive Grand Princes: Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod. By the middle of the twelfth century Kievan Rus' had dissolved into independent principalities, each ruled by a different branch of the dynasty.

A coalition of Rus' princes led by Dmitry Donskoy defeated the Mongol warlord Mamai at Kulikovo in 1380. Yet the new khan Tokhtamysh and his Rus' allies sacked Moscow in 1382, punishing it for resisting Mongol authority. Mongol domination of the Rus' principalities continued into the early 16th century.

Under Ivan III, the first central government bodies in Russia, called Prikaz, were created. The Sudebnik was also adopted, the first set of laws since the 11th century. The double-headed eagle became the coat of arms of Russia.

After the fall of Constantinople and the end of the Byzantine Empire in 1453, the Grand Dukes of Muscovy came to see themselves as successors to the Byzantine heritage. Ivan III married Sophia Paleologue, which fed the idea of Moscow as the "Third Rome". He adopted the golden Byzantine double-headed eagle on his seal, first documented in 1472.

Roman the Great united the Rurikid principalities of Galicia and Volhynia into one state after the last Prince of Galicia, Vladimir II Yaroslavich, died in 1198 or 1199 without a recognised heir in the paternal line. In 1204 he captured Kyiv in alliance with Poland, signed a peace treaty with the Kingdom of Hungary, and established diplomatic relations with the Byzantine Empire. In 1205 he turned against his Polish allies, leading to a conflict with Leszek the White and Konrad of Masovia, and he was killed at the Battle of Zawichost in 1205. His death sent Galicia–Volhynia into a period of rebellion and chaos.

Muscovite bookmen later claimed that the indecisive standoff at the Ugra in 1480 marked the end of the Tatar yoke and the liberation of Russia. Historians note that Mongol domination and tax collection by overlords such as the Crimean Khans actually continued into the early 16th century.

After Roman's death in battle, Galicia–Volhynia fell into rebellion and chaos and became an arena of rivalry between Poland and Hungary. King Andrew II of Hungary styled himself rex Galiciæ et Lodomeriæ, Latin for "king of Galicia and Vladimir [in-Volhynia]", a title later adopted by the House of Habsburg. In a compromise agreement made in 1214 between Hungary and Poland, the throne was given to Andrew's son, Coloman of Lodomeria.

The image of Saint George slaying the dragon began as a rider armed with a spear on the seal of Vasili I of Moscow in 1390. A dragon was added in the time of Ivan III. The final association with Saint George was not made until 1730, when an Imperial decree described it as such.

philosophy.text: Kievan Rus' adopted Orthodox Christianity from the Byzantine Empire in 988. Vladimir the Great adopted Christianity from Byzantium, which began a synthesis of Byzantine and Slavic cultures that would define Russian culture for the next millennium.
Religion in medieval Rus' was not always neatly divided. Elements of East Slavic paganism and Christianity overlapped, and they sometimes produced even a double faith in Muscovite Rus'.
Islam has a long history in the lands of Ukraine. It dates back to Berke Khan of the Golden Horde in the 13th century and to the establishment of the Crimean Khanate in the 15th century.

Khan Uzbek, who ruled from 1313 to 1341, officially introduced Islam as the state religion of the Crimean peninsula. He made Solkhat the administrative center of a new ulus of the Golden Horde and lived in Crimea for a time, showing his subjects a model of adherence to Islamic tenets.
Sunnism of the Hanafi school spread in Crimea. The khans of the Golden Horde were Hanafites, and the same legal school of Islam was the state religion of the Ottoman Empire.

The legendary Tamerlane (1336-1405) completed the Islamization of the Crimean population by deposing the Golden Horde Khan Tokhtamysh. After the Golden Horde period, the Crimean ulus became independent and gave rise to the Crimean Khanate, ruled from 1427 by the Gerai family.
Accurate evidence of a permanent Muslim presence in Kievan Rus' dates to the 11th century. At that time the Kiev prince had a cavalry made up of Muslim Pechenegs.

Kievan Rus' had early contact with Islam through military campaigns to the East. One was Prince Volodymyr of Kiev's campaign to Bulgar in 985, in a land where Islam had been declared the state religion in 922.
Judaism has a long history on the territory of present-day Ukraine. From the 13th century, the Ashkenazi Jewish presence in Ukraine increased significantly.

culture.text: Yaroslav the Wise, who ruled from 1019 to 1054, saw Kievan Rus' reach the zenith of its cultural development and military power. His reign also saw the creation of the state's first written legal code, the Russkaya Pravda. Together with his father Vladimir, he is credited with Kiev's Golden Age.

The steppe culture of the Cossacks originated from nomadic steppe people who merged with Eastern Slavic groups into large communities. The early Cossack communities emerged in the 14th century, the first among them being the Don Cossacks. Cossack communities later shaped many Russian songs and elements of Russian dance.

The elements of East Slavic paganism and Christianity overlapped in Rus' and sometimes produced even a double faith in Muscovite Rus'. This followed the gradual adoption of Eastern Orthodoxy through trade and cultural contact with the Byzantine Empire. Many sources say the Mongol Empire destroyed Ryazan, Kolomna, Moscow, Vladimir and Kiev, yet western Russia and the Rus' regions kept strong cultural contacts with Byzantium after the Mongol invasion.

After the Golden Horde period, the Crimean ulus separated into an independent state that became the Crimean Khanate. From 1427, the dynasty of khans from the Gerai family ruled it. Sunni Islam of the Hanafi school spread in Crimea, the same legal school that was the state religion of the Ottoman Empire.
